summary: Jean-François Desgranges was an Indology scholar who studied at the École Normale Supérieure in 1795 and under Antoine-Léonard Chézy.

Jean-François Jarrige was an archaeologist, historian, and Indologist who studied at Lycée Claude Fauriel, École du Louvre, and the University of Paris. He served as director (1986–2004) and head (~1986–2008) of the Guimet Museum.

Philosopher Jean-François Lyotard studied at Lycée Louis-le-Grand, the University of Paris, and Paris Nanterre University. He held academic posts at Prytanée National Militaire, the University of Paris, Paris Nanterre, Paris 8, UC Irvine, and Emory University.
Jean-François Revel was a philosopher who was educated at Lycée Jean-Baptiste-Say, Lycée du Parc, and the École Normale Supérieure (1943).

Jean-Jacques Bochinger specialized in religious studies and Indology, studying at Strasbourg, Heidelberg, Göttingen, and under Eugène Burnouf. In 1830, he served as a minister at the University of Strasbourg.

Jean-Jacques-Antoine Ampère worked in history, archaeology, and linguistics, studying at Lycée Henri-IV and under Eugène Burnouf. He held posts at the Athénée de Marseille, the Sorbonne, the École Normale Supérieure, and the Collège de France (1833–1864).

Linguist Jean-Louis Burnouf studied at Collège d'Harcourt, Lycée Saint-Louis, and under Alexander Hamilton and Antoine-Léonard Chézy. His major posts included professor at the Collège de France (1817–1844), master at École Normale Supérieure, and inspector at Académie de Paris.

Jean-Luc Achard is a scholar of Tibetology and Buddhist studies who was educated at the École Pratique des Hautes Études and held a post at the Centre national de la recherche scientifique (attested 2003–2004).

Jean-Luc Chevillard specializes in Indology and linguistics. He studied at the École Normale Supérieure and under Antoine Culioli, later holding posts at the Centre national de la recherche scientifique (~1993) and the University of Hamburg (~2003).

Archaeologist Jean-Marie Casal studied at the Musée du Louvre under Philippe Stern. He served with the Délégation Archéologique Française en Afghanistan (1951–1958), Musées Nationaux (1957), and the National Centre for Scientific Research (1969–1975).

Jean-Noël Robert, a scholar of Japanology, Buddhist studies, and sinology, studied at INALCO and under Bernard Frank. He held positions at the CNRS, École Pratique des Hautes Études, Institut des hautes études japonaises, and Collège de France (2011–2022).

Jean-Pierre Abel-Rémusat was a sinologist, linguist, and Buddhist studies scholar who studied under Antoine-Isaac Silvestre de Sacy. He held the Chair for Chinese at the Collège de France (1814–1832) and posts at the Bibliothèque nationale and Société Asiatique.

Sinologist and Buddhist studies scholar Jean-Pierre Drège studied at the University of Burgundy, INALCO, and under Yves Hervouet. He served as president of the École française d'Extrême-Orient from ~1998 to 2004.

Jean-Pierre de Menasce specialized in Iranian and Central Asian studies and religious studies, studying at Oxford, the Sorbonne, and under Émile Benveniste. He taught at the University of Fribourg (~1938–1948) and the École Pratique des Hautes Études (1949–1970).
Jean-Pierre-Guillaume Pauthier was a scholar of sinology and Indology who studied under Jean-Pierre Abel-Rémusat and Antoine-Léonard Chézy from ~1822 to 1832.
Jean-Sylvain Bailly was a scholar in history, archaeology, and Indology who studied at the French Academy of Sciences and became a member of the Académie Française in 1763.

Indologist Jeannette M. van Gelder studied at Leiden University and Utrecht University under Christianus Cornelis Uhlenbeck, Jean Philippe Vogel, Jacob Samuel Speyer, and Willem Caland. She served as librarian at the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences (~1925–1959).

Jeannine Auboyer worked in archaeology and Indology, studying at the École du Louvre, EPHE, and other Paris institutes. She was chief curator at the Guimet Museum (1965–1980) and held a chair at the École du Louvre (1965–1980).

Jeff Dolven studied at Yale University and Oxford. He held positions as a junior fellow at Harvard University, visiting assistant professor at Brandeis University, fellow at Trinity College, Cambridge, and professor of English at Princeton University.

Philosopher Jeff Malpas studied at the University of Auckland and Australian National University. His career includes posts at the University of New England, Murdoch University, Heidelberg University, and the University of Tasmania, where he became professor in 1999.
